% ---------------------------------------------------------------- [A] abstract (replacement)
Validation on our own simulator uses a continuous 15-minute schedule and an adopted $0.02$~mag
detectability floor, so the numbers above are benchmark values rather than \Rom{} yield forecasts.
On RMDC26, an independent GULLS simulation of the survey ($56,975$ selected events, none used
for training), the shipped checkpoint flags $35.6\%$ of single lenses as anomalous,
because that simulation's F146 observing pauses are absent from our training seasons. Fine-tuning the
same network on our own simulations, first with gap augmentation and then with finite-source single
lenses, lowers this to $4.8\%$ at the same threshold and raises planetary recall at a
$5.2\%$ single-lens false-alarm budget from $0.214$ (shipped) and
$0.295$ (gap augmentation only) to $0.390$; RMDC26 also guided that
diagnosis and the choice of checkpoint, so these values are optimistic for it. Applying our labelling
policy to RMDC26's noise-free curves, $44$--$46\%$ of its
selected planetary events carry no anomaly the policy would claim within one season, so we report
recall against both label sets. Code, weights, and reproducibility artifacts are released openly.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------- [B] Sec. limits, replacement paragraph
\paragraph{The schedule, not the sampling rate, is what the shipped model cannot survive.}
Our training grid is continuous within a season. The survey as simulated in the RMDC26 release is
not: F146 pauses for $43$--$44$~h per
$70.7$-day season, in six or seven pauses whose phases differ between its six
high-cadence seasons (only those near days 1, 35 and 69.5 recur), and the season is 1.3 days shorter
than our 72-day window. Essentially none of our training events contains an empty mid-season F146
bin, so the model's only prior for an empty token is the unrevealed future of a truncated season.
Imposing the measured pauses on our own held-out seasons, with nothing else changed, collapses the
shipped model (Table~\ref{tab:gap}): single-lens recall falls from $0.94$ to
$0.03$, mostly to \texttt{NonPSPL}, and \texttt{Flat} recall from
$0.96$ to $0.17$, mostly to \texttt{PeriodicVar}; the eruptive
and long-period variables and \texttt{NonPSPL} itself also degrade, and \texttt{NonPSPL} precision
falls from $0.72$ to $0.09$. A single gap of half an hour costs
nothing, but one gap of 1--2~h already lowers single-lens recall from $0.93$ to
$0.86$ ($100$ events per class), the lost events going to \texttt{NonPSPL}. The remedy is
an augmentation, not a new model: blanking one to eight contiguous runs of 1--12~h in every band
during a 12-epoch warm-start fine-tune of the shipped weights raises held-out macro-F1 under the
measured schedule from $0.375$ to $0.896$ with no clean-data cost
($0.915$ versus $0.915$).
Training on the pauses themselves does better still, provided they are the right pauses: drawing one of
RMDC26's six measured seasons per training example gives average precision $0.921$ under the
measured pauses against $0.911$ for random gaps, at a small clean-data cost
($0.948$ versus $0.952$), whereas training on a single season's
pauses generalises poorly to the other five ($0.568$). Both schedule arms train with the
caustic-in-gap relabel off. That rule relabels a binary as \texttt{PSPL} when the bins around its
recorded onset are blanked, but the onset records when the anomaly first becomes detectable, not where
the caustic is; with a fixed mask and the legacy 7.2-day onset grid it made $20.1\%$ of the
\texttt{NonPSPL}-labelled training events eligible for relabelling, while with random gaps it makes no
measurable difference ($0.910$ with it, $0.911$ without).
The shipped checkpoint's input contract is therefore \emph{continuous F146}; for a gapped schedule,
the gap-aware checkpoint of \S\ref{sec:gulls} is the one to use.

\begin{deluxetable*}{lcccccc}

           \colhead{Flat} & \colhead{NonPSPL} & \colhead{macro-F1}}
\startdata

% ---------------------------------------------------------------- [C] new section
\section{Cross-simulator validation on an independent \Rom{} simulation}\label{sec:gulls}

Every number so far comes from our own simulator. The Roman Galactic Exoplanet Survey Project
Infrastructure Team's RMDC26 release \citep{RGESPIT2026} is a simulation of the survey made with
GULLS \citep{Penny2013,Penny2019} by a different group, with its own implementation of the observing
schedule, photometry and Galactic population. We use it to test transfer: no RMDC26 event entered
training and no operating threshold was chosen on it. It was, however, used to diagnose the residual
false alarms, to set the upper end of the single-lens source-size prior, and to choose among
$8$ fine-tuned checkpoints scored on it (one seed each), so the numbers for the
finite-source checkpoint are the best of several on this set and are optimistic.

\subsection{Data, selection, and input contract}

RMDC26 contains $377,999$ events: $299,466$ single lenses (1S1L),
$35,647$ planetary lenses (1S2L) and $42,886$ planetary lenses with a
second source (2S2L). Every 1S2L and 2S2L event carries a planetary companion (median mass ratio
$1.4\times10^{-4}$ and $1.2\times10^{-4}$ on the scored events; similar but not identical
distributions, KS $p \sim 10^{-18}$), the source is flagged binary in $55\%$
of scored 2S2L events, and both planetary classes are pre-selected by GULLS' own detection statistic
($60$ or more for every such event). RMDC26 ships no pure binary-source class, so the
\citet{Gaudi1998} degeneracy of \S\ref{sec:sims} remains untested, and a \texttt{NonPSPL} call on a 2S2L
event may respond to its second source rather than its planet. RMDC26's anomalies are all planetary,
whereas $82\%$ of our \texttt{NonPSPL} evaluation events are
stellar-mass-ratio binaries (median $q = 0.12$), so transfer recall is not comparable to
the in-distribution completeness of \S\ref{sec:results}.

Selection uses catalogue parameters, never the model's output, and is applied identically to the
three classes. We keep events whose host single-lens peak amplitude, computed from the catalogue impact
parameter and blend fraction, is at least $0.1$~mag (the median single-lens event is
$0.063$~mag and $41\%$ pass) and whose Einstein timescale lies in
our prior's support, $1 \le t_{\rm E} \le 300$~d ($33\%$ of RMDC26 single lenses are
sub-day, against $0.31\%$ and $0.15\%$ of the planetary classes).
That leaves $100,935$ events. Of these, $56.4\%$ ($56,975$:
$33,353$ 1S1L, $11,388$ 1S2L, $12,234$ 2S2L) peak inside one of the
six high-cadence seasons and are scored; $22.0\%$ peak in one of the
$109$--$120$-day gaps between seasons (\S\ref{sec:gulls:seasons}),
$3.6\%$ before or after the survey, $17.9\%$ in one of the four
low-cadence seasons (outside our support), and $84$ lack a usable baseline. The
amplitude cut is on the \emph{host} lens: it removes most wide-orbit planets, whose host is barely
magnified ($10\%$ of 1S2L events with $s > 2$ pass, against $85\%$ at
$0.5 \le s < 2$), so the scored planetary events are dominated by resonant and central-caustic
geometries. Some scored inputs lie outside our training priors: the baseline is brighter than our
20~mag limit for $10\%$ of single lenses and $23$--$21\%$
of planetary events, and the blend fraction is below our prior's minimum for
$21$--$35\%$ of events.

The model is given the 72-day window starting at the season boundary in all three bands. The
baseline is the median F146 magnitude more than $5\,t_{\rm E}$ from the peak over the whole survey,
using the catalogue $t_0$ and $t_{\rm E}$, because the catalogue baseline in this release is offset
from the observed quiescent flux; a real-time pipeline would not have either. Observations are pooled
to one value per 15-minute epoch before binning, as the training cache is built; binning by raw
observation instead moves the shipped checkpoint's single-lens false-alarm rate by about ten points,
so the operating point is sensitive to this choice. Two sampling differences survive preprocessing:
the pauses, and partial bin occupancy, since RMDC26's colour visits displace one of eight F146 epochs
in about $34\%$ of the 2-h bins, an occupancy our training data never contain.
Setting that occupancy to full on $6,024$ real RMDC26 inputs lowers the finite-source checkpoint's
single-lens false alarms from $4.9\%$ to $3.6\%$ and its planetary recall from
$0.35$ to $0.26$: the model reads partial occupancy as mild evidence of an anomaly.
(The pattern cannot be imposed faithfully on our binned simulations, because a bin's features would
still come from all its epochs; teaching it would need augmentation before binning.)

\subsection{Results}\label{sec:gulls:results}

Table~\ref{tab:gulls} gives the single-lens false-alarm rate at the frozen operating threshold and
planetary recall at matched single-lens false-alarm budgets, on the identical $56,975$ events for
every checkpoint; the matched-budget comparison is the one a threshold shift cannot fake. The shipped
checkpoint flags $35.6\%$ of single lenses. Every flagged event is, by construction,
called \texttt{NonPSPL}; across all single lenses the model's first choice splits between
\texttt{NonPSPL} and \texttt{PeriodicVar} with almost none called \texttt{PSPL}, the signature of the
empty mid-season tokens. Gap augmentation brings the false-alarm rate to $11.6\%$. Its
residual false alarms rise monotonically with $\rho/|u_0|$, the ratio of source radius to impact
parameter, from $0.046$ for point-like sources to $0.674$ above 3.
The high-ratio bins are high-magnification events with very small $|u_0|$, not large sources: only
$43$ scored single lenses have $\rho > 1$ (99th percentile $0.29$). The
likely cause is in our generator: its single lenses were point sources while its binaries sampled a
finite source, so a finite-source single lens, whose rounded peak resembles no training \texttt{PSPL},
was read as anomalous. Adding finite-source single lenses (a uniform, achromatic disc; $\rho$
log-uniform up to 5, binaries unchanged) and fine-tuning for a further 12 epochs from the gap-aware
checkpoint lowers the rate to $4.8\%$ and the largest-ratio bin to $0.288$,
while planetary recall at the $5.2\%$ budget rises from $0.295$ to
$0.390$.
That comparison mixes two changes, the physics and 12 further epochs on a larger pool rich in
high-magnification single lenses. A control with the same pool shape, recipe and epochs but point-source
single lenses separates them: the extra training alone lowers false alarms to $6.4\%$ and
raises recall at the budget to $0.361$, and the physics then takes them to $4.8\%$
and $0.390$ (mean recall over false-alarm rates up to 30\%: $0.490$ and
$0.538$). The physics acts where the diagnosis predicts: in the two largest-ratio bins
false alarms fall from $0.410$ and $0.513$ to $0.280$ and
$0.288$, while the point-like bins barely change, and on our own finite-source held-out
only the physics restores single-lens recall for sources larger than the impact parameter
($0.22$ and $0.16$ for the control, $0.66$ and
$0.84$ with finite sources, in the 1--3 and $> 3$ bins).
Widening the \emph{binary} source-size prior at the same time was worse: false alarms
$8.7\%$ instead of $4.8\%$, recall $0.344$ instead of
$0.390$. The largest-ratio bins remain near $0.288$, so a large part of the
residual, not all of it, came from this missing physics. Among the scored single lenses, false alarms
are $11.8\%$ for baselines brighter than our 20~mag limit against $4.1\%$
inside it, which makes out-of-support brightness a candidate for part of the rest.

Training on the measured per-season pauses instead of random gaps also transfers. On one pool, with
everything else fixed, it lowers single-lens false alarms from $12.8\%$ to
$10.0\%$ and raises recall at the $5.2\%$ budget from
$0.279$ to $0.352$, and it is ahead in $6$ of the
$6$ seasons scored separately. That arm starts from the shipped weights on a natural-prior
pool; the last row of Table~\ref{tab:gulls} combines it with the finite-source single lenses.
The two gains do not add on RMDC26. The combined checkpoint differs from the finite-source one in three
ways: measured-season pauses instead of random gaps, the caustic-in-gap relabel off as in the schedule
arms, and a finite-source magnification without the small hand-off steps of the function used for the
other finite-source rows. Its planetary recall is within
$0.008$ of the finite-source checkpoint's at every budget, less than the
$0.014$--$0.023$ by which two runs of one recipe differ, and at the frozen
threshold it flags more single lenses ($6.3\%$ against $4.8\%$), mostly in the
largest-ratio bins. On our own held-out events with the measured pauses imposed it is better (average
precision $0.893$ against $0.874$), and at its own recalibrated threshold it trades
more false alarms for more recall ($2.4\%$ and $0.29$, against $1.6\%$ and
$0.24$), a different point on the same trade-off. We keep the finite-source
checkpoint, on which \S\S\ref{sec:gulls:seasons}--\ref{sec:gulls:cascade} were run.
%% PENDING (smooth-magnification control fspl5s_espl_g08, training 2026-09-11 21:32): one sentence isolating the
%% magnification function; and name ESPLMag2 / its 4-8 mmag steps in the finite-source sentence of this subsection.

Other changes did not help. Matching GULLS' noise, whose F146 errors equal ours for
sources brighter than 20th magnitude and reach $2.64$ times ours at 24--25~mag (a
$7$-fold background variance reproduces this; a global factor does not), gave a
checkpoint that was worse at every matched budget and in false alarms ($12.1\%$; recall
$0.298$), although its recall at the frozen threshold was higher; with a single seed and a
single noise level we do not attribute a mechanism. Recording the anomaly onset on a finer grid (an
attempt made before the off-by-one error in its first implementation was found) moved recall at the
$5.2\%$ budget from $0.390$ to $0.375$. Two fine-tunes with the same
recipe on different pools differ by $0.014$--$0.023$ in recall across the three
budgets; differences of that size between single-seed checkpoints are not resolved.

Removing the colour bands lowers planetary recall at matched budget by
$0.042$--$0.068$ for each of the three checkpoints ablated. The gain
does not come from the anomalies: on planetary events whose anomaly our policy can detect in F146,
colour changes recall at the $5.2\%$ budget only from $0.534$ to
$0.539$; on events without a detectable anomaly it raises the flag rate from
$0.170$ to $0.270$. We have not identified the mechanism (class-dependent
colours in RMDC26, or chromatic effects our F146 policy cannot see), so this is not evidence that the
colour bands carry anomaly information across simulators.

\begin{deluxetable*}{lcccccccc}
\tablecaption{Cross-simulator transfer on $56,975$ RMDC26 events ($33,353$ 1S1L,
$11,388$ 1S2L, $12,234$ 2S2L), identical inputs for every row. ``FA'' is the
percentage of single lenses over the frozen threshold $0.904$. ``Recall at'' columns give 1S2L
recall at the threshold that yields the stated single-lens false-alarm rate on this population (achieved
within $0.05$ points); the $5.2\%$ and $11.7\%$ budgets are
close to the frozen-threshold false-alarm rates of two earlier checkpoints (the first finite-source round,
$5.2\%$, and gap augmentation, $11.6\%$) and $2.0\%$ is a low-budget
reference, all chosen after seeing the results. The last four columns are the single-lens false-alarm
rate at the frozen threshold in bins of $\rho/|u_0|$. Fine-tunes are 12-epoch warm starts on our
simulations, one seed each: gap augmentation starts from the shipped weights, every other row from the
gap-augmented checkpoint. The last row also has the caustic-in-gap relabel off and a finite-source
magnification without hand-off steps (\S\ref{sec:gulls:results}). Generated from
\code{validation/gulls/transfer\_tradeoff\_all.json}.\label{tab:gulls}}

\startdata
shipped & 35.6 & 0.122 & 0.214 & 0.313 & 0.402 & 0.262 & 0.271 & 0.258 \\
gap augmentation (g08e12) & 11.6 & 0.185 & 0.295 & 0.457 & 0.046 & 0.429 & 0.646 & 0.674 \\
\quad + 12 epochs, point-source single lenses (control) & 6.4 & 0.244 & 0.361 & 0.485 & 0.036 & 0.208 & 0.410 & 0.513 \\
\quad + 12 epochs, finite-source single lenses & 4.8 & 0.265 & 0.390 & 0.533 & 0.031 & 0.154 & 0.280 & 0.288 \\

\enddata
\end{deluxetable*}

\paragraph{Operating point.} The frozen threshold was chosen on gap-free, point-source data. We chose
the finite-source checkpoint's threshold at the paper's 90\% purity target on our own simulated seasons
with the measured RMDC26 pauses imposed, without reading RMDC26, on a finite-source held-out pool whose
population-weighted \texttt{NonPSPL} prevalence ($6.0\%$) is close to our test set's
($5.6\%$). Using the whole pool gives $0.957$; the 20\% validation slices of the
paper's own procedure scatter between $0.942$ and $0.962$ (68\% of slices). At
$0.957$ the checkpoint flags $1.6\%$ of RMDC26 single lenses
($1.3$--$2.4\%$ across that scatter) with planetary recall
$0.24$ / $0.27$ (1S2L / 2S2L). The gap-aware checkpoint has no
usable operating point on a finite-source population: it reaches 90\% purity only on its few most
confident events.

\subsection{What ``recall'' means across two label ontologies}\label{sec:gulls:labels}

GULLS assigns classes by generator, subject to its own detection cut; BinML's classes are observational
(\S\ref{sec:detcond}). Because RMDC26 ships each event's noise-free light curve and per-epoch error, the
two can be reconciled: we applied our labelling rule, the $\Delta\chi^2$ thresholds and the $0.02$~mag
floor against the best-fitting static point-source single-lens model on the noise-free F146 curve, with
GULLS' errors as $\sigma$ and single lenses labelled exactly as in training, to the first
$1,600$ scored single lenses and $2,500$ scored events of each planetary
class. Under that rule $44\%$ of 1S2L and
$46\%$ of 2S2L events carry no anomaly the policy would claim within one season:
$26\%$ of the planetary events fail the $\Delta\chi^2$ cut and $19\%$ pass
it but fall under the floor. Rescaling the $\Delta\chi^2$ cuts for RMDC26's $11\%$ more F146 epochs per
season moves these fractions by under a point. The figure depends on the floor, the single-season window
and our selection; it is not a statement about what a survey could detect. Recall against generator
labels mixes detectable and undetectable planets and is not bounded by the detectable fraction: the
finite-source checkpoint flags $24\%$ of the planetary events without a detectable
anomaly. On those with one, its recall at the frozen threshold is $0.474$ /
$0.557$ (1S2L / 2S2L) against $0.380$ / $0.404$ on
generator labels, and $0.325$ / $0.398$ at its own operating
point. Recall is limited by significance rather than amplitude: it rises from $0.17$ for
anomalies with $160 \le \Delta\chi^2 < 500$ to $0.87$ above $10^5$.

The rule also bears on the floor. The checkpoint flags $40\%$ of the planetary events
whose anomaly is significant but below $0.02$~mag, at a similar rate however far below
($38$--$47\%$ across sub-floor amplitude bins); with F146
alone the rate falls to $16$--$20\%$, so much of it follows the
colour behaviour above. It also flags $10$ of the $20$ single
lenses whose static refit shows a significant sub-floor misfit (95\% interval
$30$--$70\%$; such misfits come from effects our static
point-source refit does not model, such as parallax): the response to sub-floor misfit is not specific
to planets. Lowering the floor from $0.02$ to
$0.005$~mag raises the fraction of 1S2L events with a claimable anomaly from $56\%$ to
$70\%$; raising it to $0.05$~mag lowers it to $40\%$. This is the
label side of the floor sensitivity; retraining under another floor is not covered here.

\subsection{Events whose peak falls between seasons}\label{sec:gulls:seasons}

The single-season input contract leaves out the $22.0\%$ of eligible events that peak in
one of the gaps between seasons, where nothing is observed. For the first $1,000$ such events of each
class we scored the high-cadence season on each side of the gap and kept the larger anomaly probability,
and applied the labelling rule of \S\ref{sec:gulls:labels} to each season, starting the single-lens refit
also at the in-window maximum because the host's peak lies outside the window. A high-cadence season
borders the gap for $76$, $91$ and $86\%$ of the
between-season 1S1L, 1S2L and 2S2L events; the rest border only low-cadence seasons. In those seasons a
claimable anomaly is visible for $44\%$ of the scorable 1S2L and $34\%$ of the
2S2L events, against $56\%$ and $54\%$ in-season, so the unobserved gap
costs $12$ and $20$ points of claimable anomalies. At the frozen threshold
the finite-source checkpoint flags $0.7\%$ of these single lenses (at most $1.6\%$ at 95\%
confidence) but recalls only $0.31$ / $0.38$ of the planetary events with a
claimable anomaly in a wing, against $0.474$ / $0.557$ in-season: a
season holding only a wing of the event looks like a quiet or slowly varying star, and the model is
conservative there. Lowering the threshold until $5.2\%$ of this population's single lenses
are flagged ($0.61$, set on only $38$ exceedances) raises that recall to
$0.50$ / $0.55$, comparable to the in-season $0.50$ /
$0.58$ at the same budget, so scoring seasons around a gap would need its own
operating point. No model can recover anomalies that fall in the unobserved gaps; what a whole-mission
model would add is events whose light curves span seasons and the four low-cadence seasons
($17.9\%$ of eligible events), which are outside BinML's support.

\subsection{The partial-season cascade on RMDC26}\label{sec:gulls:cascade}
Section~\ref{sec:cascade} measures how early the model flags an anomaly, on our own simulator and for
eligible binaries only. We repeated its primary protocol on RMDC26 with the finite-source checkpoint at the
frozen threshold. The high-cadence season of $3,000$ single lenses and $3,000$ binaries was
revealed in half-day steps, every cut was scored from F146 alone, and the alert is the first cut above the
threshold. The onset is the first cut at which our labelling rule (\S\ref{sec:gulls:labels}) is met on
GULLS' noise-free light curve with GULLS' errors, so it comes from a simulator we did not write. The
$1,667$ eligible events are the binaries whose anomaly is claimable over the whole season; nothing is
selected on the model's output.

Premature alerts stay rare: $2.2\%$ of the eligible events are flagged before the onset (95\%
interval $1.6$--$3.0\%$), against $1.4\%$ and $4.2\%$ for the
giant-planet and Neptune strata of the in-house scan ($138$ and $48$ events; shipped
model, our simulator), the only strata comparable with RMDC26's planetary anomalies. Alerts come later: the
median lag of the others is $+6.5$~d, against $+4.5$~d in-house. Detection does not
transfer: $57\%$ ($55$--$59\%$) of the eligible events are flagged by the end of the
season, against $89\%$ and $73\%$ in-house, in line with the full-season recall on
claimable anomalies ($0.474$ and $0.557$, \S\ref{sec:gulls:labels}).
Revealing all three bands lowers premature alerts to $1.4\%$ and lengthens the lag to
$+11.2$~d, as it does in-house, but it also lowers detection, to $53\%$, where
in-house it rose slightly ($89.0\%$ to $91.0\%$).

Scanning single lenses measures what the in-house scan could not: the alert burden. $5.7\%$
of single lenses raise an alert at some point in the season ($0.80$ alerts per 1,000 events
per day). If 1\% of events were planetary binaries, $5\%$ of alerts would come from a claimable
anomaly, and $21\%$ at 5\%. At RMDC26's own rate-weighted planetary fraction, which
over-represents planets, the figure is $51\%$. These count single-lens contamination only;
RMDC26 contains no variable stars or flat sources, so a real stream would be less pure. At the recalibrated
threshold single-lens alerts fall to $2.2\%$ and purity at 1\% rises to
$10\%$, but detection falls to $42\%$, premature alerts to $0.9\%$, and the
lag grows to $+8.8$~d. The cascade's low premature-alert rate therefore holds on another simulator,
but its alerts are not a follow-up list by themselves: at realistic prevalence they need a second stage that
removes single-lens contaminants.

\subsection{What this test does and does not establish}

It establishes that the shipped model's failure on a gapped schedule is a property of the schedule,
reproducible without any GULLS data and remediable by augmentation, and that a specific missing piece of
physics in our generator accounted for a large part of the remaining single-lens false alarms. It does
not establish a \Rom{} planet yield: RMDC26's planetary population, detection cut and our amplitude
selection all differ from our training population; neither simulator contains real systematics; our
detectability policy uses a static point-source refit and a uniform source without limb darkening; the
fine-tunes' gap relabelling is approximate (\S\ref{sec:sims}); every fine-tune is a single seed; and
RMDC26 was used to choose among checkpoints. It does not test the binary-source degeneracy, for which
RMDC26 has no class. Sub-day single lenses, outside our timescale prior, are rarely flagged as anomalies
by the finite-source checkpoint ($0.7\%$ of $1,385$ unweighted,
$3.1\%$ weighted by event rate) but are read mostly as periodic variables
($60$--$93\%$ across checkpoints), not as microlensing; a model for
free-floating planets needs sub-day timescales in its prior, not a threshold change.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------- [D] Discussion paragraph
BinML's input is one contiguous season. On RMDC26 that contract leaves out a fifth of the selected events,
those peaking between seasons, and another $17.9\%$ that peak in low-cadence seasons.
Scoring the high-cadence seasons around a gap recovers most of the former at a false-alarm cost below
one percent, but a claimable anomaly survives in a wing for fewer planetary events than in-season and the
operating point would have to be set separately (\S\ref{sec:gulls:seasons}); the latter are outside the
model's support. A whole-mission model, taking the full light curve, would address both and let the
partial-season cascade of \S\ref{sec:cascade} run across season boundaries. It needs a mission-length
simulation, labels over the full mission and a hierarchical input, and is the natural next version.
